Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 108, verses 1–3:

(p-354) Surat al-Kawthar

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾. Regarding it there are nine interpretations. The first: al-Kawthar is prophethood. This was said by Ikrimah.

The second: it is the Qur'an. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: it is Islam. This was related by al-Mughirah.

The fourth: it is a river in Paradise, related from Ibn Umar and Anas, marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ).

The fifth: it is the Basin (hawd) of the Prophet ﷺ at which people will crowd on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ata'.(p-355)

The sixth: it is abundant good. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The seventh: it is the abundance of his Ummah. This was said by Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash.

The eighth: it is generosity (al-iithar). This was said by Ibn Kaysan.

The ninth: it is the elevation of his remembrance, and it is on the pattern fawal from kathrah (abundance).

﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾. Regarding it there are three sayings. The first: the obligatory prayer, which is the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the prayer of the feast. This was said by Ata'.

The third: its meaning is "give thanks to your Lord." This was said by Ikrimah.

As for ﴿and sacrifice﴾, there are five interpretations. The first: "and sacrifice your offering (hady) or your sacrificial animal (udhiyyah)." This was said by Ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: "and sacrifice," meaning "and ask." This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: its meaning is to place the right hand upon the left at his nahr (chest) during the prayer. This was said by Ali and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The fourth: to raise his hands in the takbir. This was related by Ali.

The fifth: he intended "and face the qiblah in prayer with your nahr," said by Abu al-Ahwas, and from it is the poet's verse:(p-356)

"O Abu Hakam, are you not the paternal uncle of Mujalid, and the lord of the people of al-Abtah, the mutanahir?"

That is, the mutaqabil (facing one another).

﴿Indeed, your enemy (shani'ak) is the one cut off (al-abtar)﴾. Regarding shani'ak there are two meanings. One: your hater (mubghidak), said by Ibn Shajarah. The second: your enemy (aduwwuk), said by Ibn Abbas.

Regarding "al-abtar" there are five interpretations. The first: it is the lowly and humiliated one. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is the solitary, lone one. This was said by Ikrimah.

The third: it is the one in whom there is no good, until he becomes like the abtar (one cut off). This is a transmitted saying.

The fourth: the Quraysh used to say of one whose male offspring had died, "So-and-so has been cut off (buttira)." When the son of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, al-Qasim, died in Makkah, and Ibrahim in Madinah, they said, "Muhammad has been cut off; he has no one to take charge of his affair after him." So the verse was revealed. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: when Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he called Quraysh to faith, they said, "Muhammad has ibtatar from us," meaning he opposed us and cut himself off from us. Allah, may He be exalted, then informed His Messenger that they are the ones who are cut off. This was said by Ikrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab.

Scholars differed about whom the phrase "Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off" refers to among Quraysh, in three sayings. The first: it is Abu Lahab. This was said by Ata'. The second: Abu Jahl. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The third: it is al-As ibn Wa'il. This was said by Ikrimah. And Allah knows best.
